Cuneiform. This is one of the earliest known writing systems, originating in ancient Mesopotamia around thirty-four hundred BCE and consisting of wedge-shaped marks impressed into clay tablets. Developed by the Sumerians, cuneiform was adapted by Akkadian scribes for their Semitic language and spread throughout the ancient Near East, serving as the primary writing system for millennia and recording the earliest known literature.

Cuneiform originated as a system of pictographs, picture symbols used to record inventory and transactions, then evolved into increasingly abstract wedge-shaped impressions made with a stylus on soft clay. The name cuneiform comes from Latin cuneus meaning wedge and forma meaning shape, reflecting the characteristic wedge-shaped marks that form its letters as a consequence of using a reed stylus on clay. Akkadian scribes adapted cuneiform to write their Semitic language, replacing Sumerian as the dominant language of Mesopotamia and bureaucracy. Cuneiform could represent both logograms, word-symbols, and phonetic signs.

Cuneiform was the writing system for major ancient texts including the Code of Hammurabi, the Epic of Gilgamesh, and countless administrative records, contracts, and royal inscriptions. The wedge-shapes of cuneiform made it difficult to inscribe on surfaces other than clay, constraining its spread compared to later alphabetic systems like Phoenician writing. Cuneiform remained in use for over three thousand years, gradually displaced by alphabetic scripts, particularly Aramaic, around the first millennium BCE, though Akkadian cuneiform persisted in Assyria until the destruction of Nineveh in six hundred twelve BCE.

Cuneiform's complexity required years of scribal training. Clay tablets were fragile but also remarkably durable, especially if accidentally fired, preserving ancient texts for archaeological discovery millennia later.
